content.intro: This lesson focuses on private networking and specialized execution. content.why_it_matters: Private Networking and Specialized Execution matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Private-network jobs need tightly segmented access to internal services, and they should run only on appropriately protected runners with narrow routing rules. Self-hosted runners provide control but widen the operational responsibility. Restrict access, isolate trust levels, patch images, remove residual state, and monitor fleet health.

content_blocks.code:
name: Internal connectivity check
on: workflow_dispatch
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  internal-check:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, x64, private-network]
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - name: Verify approved endpoint access
        env:
          INTERNAL_HEALTH_URL: ${{ vars.INTERNAL_HEALTH_URL }}
        run: curl --fail --silent --show-error --max-time 10 "$INTERNAL_HEALTH_URL"
content_blocks.expected_output: The job is eligible only for a runner matching all labels; private network access depends on the runner/network configuration.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use only a test runner and health endpoint that you are authorized to access.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Never route untrusted pull-request workloads onto a privileged private-network runner.

troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
